newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative MPs defy party call to step down.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative MPs defy party call to step down.

text.p: Two Conservative members of parliament embroiled in sleaze allegations looked set to infuriate leaders of Britain's ruling party on Sunday by defying heavy pressure to step down.

Several newspapers said Prime Minister John Major, alarmed that the sleaze issue was still leading the news ahead of a general election on May 1, had made it clear that Neil Hamilton and Piers Merchant should step down.
"Mr Major is distraught at the way it has dominated the agenda and is desperate to go on the attack, but it is impossible," a senior aide told the Express on Sunday.
"We have to get it done and get it done fast. They must be out of the way before the (Conservative election) manifesto is published on Wednesday."
But both Hamilton and Merchant appeared determined to stay, even though this could hand the opposition Labour party more ammunition in its bid to win power for the first time in 18 years.

The Conservative party's chairman in Scotland, Sir Michael Hirst, resigned on Saturday because of a "personal indiscretion," hours before newspapers printed allegations about his relationship with a young male researcher.
Hirst was the third senior Conservative to quit in a week dominated by money and sexual scandals as the Conservatives were thwarted in their attempts to dent Labour's 25 point lead in opinion polls.
Senior party officials have clearly indicated that they want Merchant to step down from the safe seat of Beckenham after newspapers alleged he had an affair with a 17-year-old nightclub hostess.
But a meeting of local party officials decided he had been framed and should stand again in the elction, a decision roundly condemned by the usually pro-Conservative News of the World tabloid.

"Do they think the newspapers are making it all up, pictures and all?" it asked. "Or is the truth that the Beckenham hierarchy are blind to the interests of John Major and family? Blind to the native intelligence and decency of the voter in the street?
"Either way, these arrogant bigwigs will get the answer they deserve on May 1."

Hamilton, a former junior minister Hamilton accused of taking thousands of pounds in cash to ask questions in parliament, was in defiant mood, handing over documents to the Sunday Telegraph which he said proved his innocence.

Bookmakers William Hill dropped its odds on a Labour election victory to just six-to-one on, the shortest they have been since the party lost power in 1979, and offered odds of 11-to-one against Major's re-election.
A poll in the News of the World said Labour had a 40 percent lead among people who would be voting for the first time while a Mail on Sunday survey said it enjoyed a 22 percent lead among women.
